Finally, Chapter 7 summarizes the results of the project, open-source releases, commercializationandoutreachefforts,anddirectionsforfuturework. 3 CHAPTER2 CREATIONOFOPEN-SOURCEMICROGRIDMODELSINMODELICA 2.1 Introduction The electric power grid is undergoing a profound transition driven by the rapid growth of inverter-baseddistributedenergyresources(DER),increasingelectrification,andheightened expectationsforresiliencyinthefaceofdisturbancesandextremeevents. Traditionalpower systemswerebuiltaroundlargesynchronousmachineswhosedynamics,inertialcharacteris- ticsandcontrolbehaviorsarewellunderstood;incontrast,today’sgridsdependincreasingly on fast, power-electronics–interfaced generation whose internal control loops, limited fault current contributions, and sensitivity to grid conditions introduce new modeling and oper- ational challenges. These emerging complexities have intensified the need for modeling frameworkscapableofrepresentingcyber-physicalenergysystemswithsufficientfidelityto captureinteractionsacrosselectrical,mechanical,thermal,andcontroldomains. Becauseex- perimentation on real grids is constrained by reliability requirements and potential financial risks, simulation has become a primary mechanism for evaluating new architectures, vali- dating DER controls, and assessing microgrid performance under a wide range of operating scenarios. Inthiscontext,theModelicamodelinglanguageandtheOpenIPSLlibraryaresignificantfor developing transparent, modular, and physics-based representations of modern power sys- tems. Their equation-based formulation and object-oriented structure allow users to capture device-level behaviors, embed manufacturer-agnostic control logic, and extend models for customized applications. This chapter leverages these capabilities to develop a comprehen- sive suite of dynamic models for renewable energy sources (RES), multi-domain electrical loads, and complete microgrid systems. Beginning with the implementation of generic re- newable energy models, such as PV, wind, and battery energy storage systems (BESS), this work demonstrates how Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC)-based control structures can be reproduced in the phasor domain and validated against industry-standard tools.
